records.name: Antibody-drug conjugate (ADC)
records.tldr: An antibody-drug conjugate links a target-binding antibody to an active drug. Binding, delivery, release and drug action each matter, and normal tissues can also be exposed.
records.summary: The antibody recognizes an accessible antigen; the attachment chemistry and linker affect stability and release; the payload acts through its own molecular mechanism. Cytotoxic examples include TOP1 inhibitors, tubulin inhibitors and DNA-damaging agents. Uptake and lysosomal processing are important for many constructs, while some linkers also release drug outside cells. A surface antigen can be a delivery address without being a driver the tumor depends on. The dose, mean loading, loading distribution, released species and exposure must be interpreted for the finished product. There is no universal fold improvement in the therapeutic window.

notes: The treatment and diagnostic labels retain product-specific indications and testing requirements. A companion diagnostic validated for one drug or intended use is not automatically interchangeable with another. Keep the study population, comparator and prior exposure with any clinical result; a binding result or shared antigen name does not transfer benefit.

Follow the complete construct through separate measurements. Controlled binding to viable cells tests an accessible recognition feature; fixed-tissue staining alone does not. A trafficking assay must distinguish surface-bound from internal material. Measuring the relevant released payload or catabolite at its site of action tests a later step, and a payload-appropriate functional readout and survival over time answer further questions. A fluorescent antibody-associated tag can remain detectable without demonstrating that active drug reached that compartment. Keep assay sensitivity, time, concentration, cellular denominator and controls with each result; no one of these measurements establishes delivery throughout a tumour or clinical benefit.

In a fictional model, a tissue stain names protein M and controlled live-cell tests show antibody binding. Four proposed products still need different experiments: a blocking antibody needs a relevant signal and survival readout; a conjugate needs active-material delivery and a response to that material; an engager needs useful T cells, target-negative and no-T-cell controls, and completed target-cell killing; a radiolabelled product needs distribution over time and tumour and normal-organ dosimetry. The observed binding does not supply those unmeasured results. A model can also omit normal tissues, immune cells, spatial variation or clinically achievable exposure.

Choosing a surface address involves its measured amount, accessible normal-tissue distribution, behaviour with the actual format and variation within and between lesions. One positive core at one date cannot survey the whole tumour. A static receptor count and a manufactured loading ratio do not alone determine cumulative delivery across receptor turnover, repeated encounters and release over time. ADC uptake and processing are construct-specific; antibody retention can matter to radiation delivery, and engager contact geometry and useful effectors matter to immune recruitment. No universal antigen-density cutoff or low-density format ranking follows from a platform name. Damelin's 2015 survey found a broad range of normal- and tumour-tissue expression among the ADC targets studied and could not formalise optimal target parameters within that set. It does not show that useful target selection is impossible.

A change of format is a new product hypothesis. If an ADC binds M but yields little active material after uptake, an M-directed engager might avoid that particular processing requirement. It still needs its own binding and contact-geometry measurements, useful effector access and function, normal-tissue testing and clinical evidence. Earlier antibody or ADC tolerability does not establish the safety of a different action. Bystander delivery and two-address designs are possible responses to heterogeneous expression, not guaranteed coverage or an exhaustive list of solutions.

Compare requirements rather than rank formats. Trastuzumab can inhibit proliferation and recruit antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity; the related HER2 antibody in trastuzumab deruxtecan carries a TOP1-inhibitor payload. An ADC and a surface T-cell engager differ in processing versus productive contact with useful effectors. An engager recruits responders, whereas a CAR-T product supplies engineered living cells with their own survival, expansion and trafficking. A radioligand's carrier distribution and radiation deposition differ from chemical-payload delivery. Sharing an address does not equalise any of these actions, exposure histories or normal-tissue risks. With a clinical claim, record disease, biomarker definition, prior care, comparator, endpoint, follow-up and harms alongside the actual product; access or eligibility cannot supply an unmeasured efficacy comparison.

Four U.S. breast-cancer label examples separate address from payload: sacituzumab govitecan pairs TROP2 with SN-38, datopotamab deruxtecan pairs TROP2 with DXd, trastuzumab deruxtecan pairs HER2 with DXd, and trastuzumab emtansine pairs HER2 with DM1. SN-38 and DXd inhibit TOP1; DM1 acts on microtubules. Their indication and testing requirements differ, including the HER2-positive uses of T-DM1 and specified lower-expression uses of T-DXd. Changing the address or payload changes a design feature, not a measured probability of response. These examples are not an exhaustive U.S. or worldwide approval inventory.

Lymphoma: binding and antigen abundance do not by themselves establish usable payload delivery. Internalization, intracellular processing and payload transport need construct-specific evidence. CD20 is not universally non-internalizing: rituximab-CD20 uptake varied with target-cell Fc-gamma receptor IIb in the cited experiments. Lysosomal-transporter experiments with other conjugates also show that a block after uptake can cause resistance. These observations do not establish one limiting toxicity for all lymphoma ADCs.
records.principle: Binding can support delivery, but uptake, processing, access to the payload’s target and cellular response require separate evidence.

records.name: ADC analytes and exposure
records.tldr: An antibody-drug conjugate and its released drug do not follow one shared concentration curve. The measured chemical form matters.
records.summary: A conjugate assay measures antibody carrying payload, or antibody-bound drug, according to the validated method. Total antibody includes conjugated and unconjugated antibody; unconjugated payload measures released drug separately. Active metabolites or catabolites can add further relevant species. Concentration, time course and exposure therefore belong to a named analyte. A conjugate dose in milligrams per kilogram is not the same quantity as the mass of free payload reaching a tumor or the blood.

notes: FDA’s 2024 guidance for cytotoxic small-molecule ADCs recommends validated measurements of the conjugate and relevant constituent parts, with later omissions justified by pharmacology, assay sensitivity and exposure data. It does not require every conceivable analyte in every study or automatically apply to every immune agonist or other cargo.

For a construct carrying different payloads, keep each chemical identity, loading distribution, release behavior and exposure distinct. A manufactured loading ratio does not establish the ratio reaching tissue over time. The same total DAR does not establish equal loading of each component or equal biological activity.

The June 2026 U.S. TRODELVY label describes serum measurements in metastatic breast cancer and reports a median conjugate elimination half-life of 6.5 days and a median free-SN-38 value of 22 hours; it separately gives a 6.7-day terminal conjugate value and a 24-hour apparent free-SN-38 value. The ENHERTU label, in patients with cancer, reports median elimination half-lives of 5.4 to 5.7 days for the conjugate and 5.4 to 6.1 days for DXd. DATROWAY reports median elimination half-life 4.8 days for the conjugate and median apparent half-life about 5.5 days for released DXd. Keep the label version, named analyte, population, assay specimen and exact parameter definition; these label entries do not specify every assay matrix. The TRODELVY section presents parameters as means unless specified otherwise, so its separately labelled median, terminal and apparent values must not be merged. Similar half-life values also do not make entire concentration curves identical or measure intracellular exposure throughout a tumour.

An apparent released-drug curve can reflect continued formation as well as removal. PADCEV explicitly describes unconjugated MMAE elimination as limited by release from its conjugate. That product example is not an estimate of isolated DXd elimination. ENHERTU reports systemic clearances of 0.4 litres per day for the conjugate and 18 litres per hour for DXd; a clearance comparison alone does not determine intrinsic half-life without distribution and model information. Nakada and colleagues, working at Daiichi Sankyo, described short systemic DXd half-life as a preclinical design rationale in 2019. Their rationale and later human label parameters answer different questions and do not by themselves establish tumour selectivity or safety.

In a fictional report, antibody-associated signal remains measurable two weeks after administration. That supports detection of the measured antibody species at the sampled sites and times, not active payload in every cancer cell. Ask which chemical species the assay distinguishes, whether active material reached its action compartment, and whether a relevant functional effect and later survival were measured. Sparse blood samples and a bulk tumour sample cannot establish every cell's exposure.

records.name: ADC sequencing
records.tldr: ADC sequencing asks whether a second conjugate can help after the first fails, especially when it carries the same payload class. The earlier response and reason for stopping matter.
records.summary: A second conjugate may retain activity after a first, but neither shared nor different target names settle the outcome. Payload cross-resistance, altered delivery and tumor evolution can all matter. Retrospective treatment sequences are affected by who lived long enough and remained fit to receive another drug, treatment line, prior response and clinician selection. A selected cohort with post-treatment plasma profiling and laboratory TOP1-mutant experiments supports a resistance hypothesis; cell and mouse payload-switching experiments test a different question. Neither design establishes the best clinical sequence.

notes: Mechanism experiments can compare an intact conjugate with its free payload, measure uptake and released species, and perturb a suspected transporter or resistance gene. These experiments require controls and do not by themselves validate a clinical test for choosing the next ADC. A trial in ADC-naive patients cannot establish effectiveness specifically after progression on a prior TOP1 ADC.

Three fictional resistant models motivate different tests. If M is lost but the active payload still works with verified delivery to its action site, investigate another accessible address and the finished product's delivery. If M remains but the tested TOP1 material does not work while a microtubule-directed material does, investigate another action rather than predicting a probability of failure for every TOP1 ADC. If a pump inhibitor restores activity, test the specific export hypothesis with suitable controls: the inhibitor can have other effects. PADCEV's label identifies MMAE as a P-glycoprotein substrate, so a microtubule class name alone does not promise escape from export.

A fictional report of 25% responses after a prior ADC needs the response denominator and duration, actual earlier agents and payload classes, the reason for stopping, target entry criteria, dose and harms. Retained M supports a measured address, not an automatic bypass or a safety advantage. A shorter response on a later treatment does not by itself identify cross-resistance; disease history and selection into later therapy also matter. A comparison matched to progression on a prior TOP1 ADC answers a different question from activity in ADC-naive patients. The two cited mechanism studies do not themselves randomise patients to a payload-switch strategy; that is a bounded description of those studies, not a claim that no such trial exists.

records.name: Antibody
records.tldr: A typical IgG antibody has antigen-binding arms and a stem that can interact with other parts of the immune system. Binding alone does not specify its function.
records.summary: A typical IgG has two antigen-binding arms; receptor binding and cross-reactivity depend on the particular molecule and test system, while its stem (the Fc region) can recruit immune cells and complement or extend the antibody's life in the blood. Therapeutic antibodies block growth receptors (trastuzumab on HER2, cetuximab on EGFR), release the brakes on T cells (pembrolizumab on PD-1), flag cancer cells for immune killing (rituximab on CD20), or serve as the targeting vehicle of ADCs and radioimmunotherapy. Bispecific formats have two binding specificities. Some are designed to bring a T cell and a target cell together; their structures and functions vary. Fab, the arm with the binding site, and Fc, the stem, are separate parts: binding does not guarantee killing, and Fc effector contacts need compatible effector cells or complement. Antibodies that bind the same target can act differently: a blocking antibody, an antibody-drug conjugate and a bispecific format can share a target and still differ in what follows.

records.name: Antibody structure (Fab, Fc and hinge)
records.tldr: An antibody has tips that find a target and a stem that can connect to other parts of the immune system. Two antibodies can reach the same target and do different jobs.
records.summary:
A typical immunoglobulin G (IgG) antibody has two heavy and two light chains held together by molecular interactions and disulfide bonds. At each arm tip, variable regions from a heavy and a light chain together form a binding site; its sequence and three-dimensional shape influence what it recognises. Fab (fragment antigen-binding) names an arm containing the binding site and its associated constant domains, so it is not simply another word for the variable region. Fc (fragment crystallizable, a name that comes from an experimental property) names the remaining stem, built from CH2 and CH3 domains of both heavy chains in the familiar IgG description. Hinge flexibility changes how the arms are arranged. A drawn Y is a simplification: some natural and engineered formats omit familiar parts.

Fc can interact with immune-cell receptors and with complement, but compatible effectors, target arrangement and other conditions decide whether killing, engulfment or complement damage follows, so Fc is not an automatic kill command. Binding and effector contributions are separate and the finished molecule needs testing. Nimmerjahn and Ravetch (2005) showed in mouse experiments that IgG subclasses differ in the ratio of their binding to activating and inhibitory Fc receptors, which predicted in vivo activity; that is not a universal ranking of human antibody performance. An isotype is a heavy-chain class (see the isotypes and Fc silencing record). Structure alone does not identify the producing cell or establish what the antibody recognises.

The epitope is the molecular feature recognised and can be a folded protein surface or another accessible feature, not necessarily a short fragment displayed by HLA. Binding is measured against a defined antigen preparation and antibody concentration, sometimes in nanomoles per litre, and it matters whether the test used purified protein or intact cells, because folding, accessibility and multiple binding sites change the result. A concentration or fluorescence signal alone is not an affinity. Fc-receptor and complement interactions are tested separately from target binding, and neither binding nor a laboratory effector result establishes clinical benefit or safety. A blocking antibody, an antibody-drug conjugate and a bispecific format can share a target and still act differently.

records.name: ASCENT
records.tldr: ASCENT compared sacituzumab govitecan with single-agent chemotherapy in previously treated metastatic triple-negative breast cancer. The primary analysis excluded patients with brain metastases.
records.summary:
ASCENT (NCT02574455), published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2021, randomised 529 patients overall. The primary population comprised 468 without brain metastases. Sacituzumab govitecan improved progression-free and overall survival compared with physician’s-choice single-agent chemotherapy in that population. The randomised comparison does not establish equal effects at every TROP2 expression level.

A prespecified exploratory biomarker analysis had TROP2 data for 290 of the 468 primary-population patients. The authors supported benefit in the high and medium groups and considered the low group too small for a definitive conclusion. The absence of a TROP2 label-selection requirement is a separate regulatory fact. Post hoc demographic and brain-metastasis analyses retain their own populations and uncertainty; none is a prospective validation of a universal marker cutoff.

notes: The 2021 primary report gives progression-free survival of 5.6 versus 1.7 months and overall survival of 12.1 versus 6.7 months in the population without brain metastases. All 468 participants in the original primary population without brain metastases had previously received a taxane. The 2021 progression-free and overall-survival results belong to that previously treated metastatic population; they are not a comparison between two ADCs or evidence for postoperative use or use after a specified prior TOP1 conjugate.

Design (NEJM 2021): 529 patients with relapsed or refractory metastatic triple-negative disease after at least two prior therapies randomised 1 to 1 to sacituzumab govitecan 10 mg/kg on days 1 and 8 of 21 or physician's choice of eribulin, vinorelbine, capecitabine or gemcitabine; 468 without brain metastases formed the primary population. Post hoc subgroups (npj Breast Cancer 2024) reported longer progression-free and overall survival in the examined older and Black participant groups; these were exploratory comparisons, not prospective marker-interaction tests. In the stable-brain-metastasis subgroup, progression-free survival was numerically longer but overall survival similar.

records.tldr: B7-H3 expression is an assay result. A positive stain does not by itself establish drug activity, safety or eligibility.
records.summary: B7-H3, also called CD276, has been studied on cancer cells and tumour-associated vessels. Expression in a tissue sample is different from accessible binding, delivered active material and clinical benefit. Preclinical compartment-targeting experiments and clinical trial registrations answer different questions; neither supplies a universal expression threshold or a breast-cancer prevalence estimate.

records.name: Bispecific ADC
records.tldr: A bispecific antibody-drug conjugate uses two recognition features to deliver a payload. Its design can change delivery; phase 3 testing still evaluates the complete drug.
records.summary: Different-antigen designs recognize two proteins; biparatopic designs recognize distinct epitopes on one protein. Depending on the molecule and cell, the design may favor binding to either target, combined binding, receptor clustering or transport through an internalizing partner. A biparatopic HER2 conjugate carrying a tubulysin derivative promoted clustering and lysosomal trafficking in preclinical models. A separate HER2-by-prolactin-receptor study increased uptake and cell killing by linking a slower-trafficking target to a rapidly internalized partner. These experiments do not isolate a universal clinical advantage of two-target binding. Clinical examples need their own evidence: the registry identifies izalontamab brengitecan (EGFR-by-HER3) in the phase 3 BL-B01D1-307/PANKU-Breast02 study of previously treated advanced triple-negative breast cancer against chemotherapy. That design does not isolate the added contribution of the bispecific format over another ADC.

A second recognition feature is one way to investigate delivery, not the only one. Changes to a linker, released species, carrier properties or exposure can also change which cells receive active material. A new binding design must be tested as a finished product rather than inheriting the original binder's behaviour. A favourable result with one target pair does not establish a universal low-density advantage or prove that no other design could address the observed failure.

records.name: Bystander effect (ADC)
records.tldr: A conjugate can harm neighboring cells when an active released species reaches them, including neighbors with little or none of the delivery target.
records.summary: Bystander killing is a local drug effect, distinct from radiation crossfire or immune memory. It depends on the chemical species actually released, its transport through membranes and tissue, the concentration reaching neighboring cells and their susceptibility. Ogitani and colleagues compared a permeable DXd species, a poorly permeable alternative and the T-DM1 catabolite Lys-SMCC-DM1. Their coculture and mixed-tumor mouse experiments showed neighboring target-negative-cell killing with the permeable DXd construct; a separate target-negative tumor on the opposite flank did not respond in that experiment. These findings support a local mechanism in those models, not a universal safety or patient-benefit claim.

notes: Neither a cleavable-linker label nor a permeability result alone proves bystander killing in a tumor. More chemical spread can also expose normal cells, so it is not an efficacy ranking.

records.name: CAR-T cell therapy
records.tldr: CAR-T therapy uses T cells carrying an engineered receptor. Approved products treat selected blood cancers, with product-specific eligibility and safety requirements.
records.summary:
CAR-T cell therapy uses T cells carrying a chimeric antigen receptor to recognize a target. FDA-approved products include CD19- and BCMA-directed CAR-T cells for selected blood cancers, including B-cell leukemias, lymphomas and multiple myeloma. The individual product label defines the treatment setting and eligibility. A common autologous approach collects a person’s T cells, engineers and expands them outside the body, then infuses them back; conditioning and follow-up depend on the protocol.

A common antibody-derived CAR joins an external binding region, a hinge or spacer, a membrane anchor and intracellular signaling domains. The receptor is a protein; its encoding instructions and the living cell carrying it are different objects. Approved products and experimental constructs differ in cell source, receptor, manufacturing and clinical setting. Product labels and trial records define their actual uses; a platform name does not establish eligibility or benefit.

In early work, Gross, Waks and Eshhar joined antibody-variable regions to T-cell receptor components in 1989. Eshhar and colleagues subsequently tested single-chain antibody-binding regions joined to gamma or zeta signaling chains in 1993. These experimental designs helped separate recognition from the signaling machinery attached to it.

FDA-approved examples include tisagenlecleucel, axicabtagene ciloleucel, lisocabtagene maraleucel, brexucabtagene autoleucel, obecabtagene autoleucel, idecabtagene vicleucel and ciltacabtagene autoleucel. Their labeled diseases, treatment settings and eligibility differ; the individual product records retain those distinctions.

notes: Generation labels describe common signaling architectures. First-generation constructs use an activation domain, often CD3 zeta; second-generation designs add one costimulatory region; third-generation designs combine two. Fourth-generation and later labels vary across authors. More domains do not establish better patient outcomes. The full binder, spacer, anchor, signaling arrangement and cell preparation still matter.

CD28 and 4-1BB are borrowed intracellular signaling regions, not separately administered receptors. Kawalekar compared metabolic and memory features in defined human-cell experiments. Ramos co-infused two specified second- and third-generation products in lymphoma; different expansion and persistence did not isolate comparative clinical benefit. Neither study ranks all products by signaling-domain name.

Binding, surface CAR expression, activation, proliferation and completed target-cell killing are distinct readouts. Compare otherwise matched constructs, target-positive and target-negative cells, healthy-tissue targets and unstimulated activity. Hudecek found that particular IgG-derived spacers could support killing in a dish yet impair activity in mouse models through Fc interactions.

A peptide-HLA target is an exception to blanket HLA-independent descriptions. Rafiq tested a WT1 peptide presented by HLA-A*02:01 in cell and mouse models; this was a proof of concept, not evidence that every intracellular protein or every HLA type is addressable by that construct.

A 2024 preprint used a pooled signaling-domain library, repeated stimulation and single-cell sequencing to study how domain arrangement affected T-cell states over time. Its membrane-proximal-domain findings are construct-and-assay observations, not a clinical ranking of domains or a validation of pooled-screen hits as treatments.

FDA initiated boxed-warning changes in 2024 for the risk of T-cell malignancies after the then-approved BCMA- or CD19-directed autologous CAR T-cell products. Its communication calls for lifelong monitoring for secondary malignancies. This is a scoped regulatory warning, not a claim that every type of engineered immune cell has the same risk.

In June 2025, FDA eliminated REMS requirements for the named autologous CAR T-cell products in its notice. Product warnings and safety monitoring continued. The manufacturer postmarketing observational studies with 15-year follow-up described in that notice are different from the lifelong patient-monitoring statement in the earlier safety communication.

Relapse mechanisms need separate investigation. Sotillo found CD19 sequence and splicing changes affecting recognition in B-ALL relapse material and experiments. Deng found infusion-product transcriptional features associated with outcomes in a selected cohort of 24 large B-cell lymphoma infusion products; those associations did not prove that one engineered modification would correct every failure.
records.principle: A common CAR presents a binder outside the cell and signaling domains inside it, connected through a spacer and transmembrane region. Conventional surface-antigen recognition can bypass peptide-HLA presentation; specialized peptide-HLA-targeting CARs retain the relevant HLA and antigen-processing requirements.

records.name: Cross-resistance
records.tldr: Resistance to one treatment can also reduce sensitivity to another when the treatments share a vulnerable step. A different drug name does not establish an independent mechanism.
records.summary: For antibody-drug conjugates, resistance can involve antigen access or uptake, intracellular processing and transport, the payload’s molecular target, drug efflux, or the cell’s response to injury. Breast cancer models selected for resistance to T-DXd or sacituzumab govitecan showed shared payload-associated resistance and renewed activity with some non-TOP1 conjugates. A selected patient cohort and functional experiments also linked particular TOP1 mutations to reduced sensitivity to SN-38 and deruxtecan. These are distinct forms of evidence, not proof that every resistant tumor has the same cause or that switching class improves outcomes for everyone.

notes: Changing the antibody target can leave shared efflux or cell-response resistance intact. Changing payload mechanism can leave a delivery or processing defect intact. A transporter may handle more than one drug, and different tumor cells can carry different resistance mechanisms. Collateral sensitivity is the separate possibility that adaptation to one treatment increases sensitivity to another.

Abelman's 2025 selected institutional cohort had paired plasma testing around ADC progression: TOP1 variants were found in 4 of 31 patients, compared with 3 of 420 patients not treated with an ADC. Three of the four variants were not detected before ADC treatment; one, S57C, was already detectable. Assay non-detection is not proof that a variant did not previously exist. Functional experiments with specified mutant proteins add a separate resistance test. Rampa's 2026 work selected resistant breast cell lines and tested conjugates in those cells and nude-mouse xenografts; changing to tested MMAF constructs restored activity in those models. These observations do not establish the cause of every patient's resistance or a beneficial clinical payload-switch strategy.

Delivery, active-payload action and cellular response can organise questions about failure, but they are not independent or validated clinical cause categories. A tumour can combine altered recognition or processing, export, a changed payload target, and repair or tolerance of injury. Sampling one site, time or plasma assay can miss other cells and mechanisms. A new address may leave a payload vulnerability intact; another payload may leave a delivery problem intact. The next discriminating test must examine the proposed explanation rather than infer it from the treatment name.

records.name: Drug-to-antibody ratio (DAR)
records.tldr: DAR usually reports the average number of payload molecules attached per antibody. The average can hide a mixture of differently loaded molecules.
records.summary: Drug-to-antibody ratio describes payload loading. A preparation can contain antibodies with different numbers and sites of attachment, so the reported mean does not specify every molecule. Two preparations with the same mean can differ in their loading distribution and attachment chemistry. Higher loading can increase cell-assay potency while also changing hydrophobicity, aggregation, clearance and tolerated exposure. Hamblett and colleagues separated differently loaded versions of one anti-CD30 conjugate and found that greater cell-assay potency did not translate into a proportional mouse treatment advantage. That experiment does not set one optimal DAR for every product.

records.name: Drug target and mechanism of action
records.tldr: A drug target is the molecule or structure a treatment acts on and its mechanism of action is how that action produces an effect, and each step from target to patient benefit needs its own evidence.
records.summary:
A drug target is a biological molecule or structure that a treatment acts on, and the mechanism of action explains how that action produces an effect. The National Cancer Institute describes targeted therapy as treatment that targets proteins that control how cancer cells grow, divide and spread, and says most targeted therapies are small-molecule drugs, which are small enough to enter cells and so suit targets inside cells, or monoclonal antibodies, which are designed to attach to specific targets on cancer cells. It describes antibodies that mark cancer cells for the immune system, antibodies that stop growth or cause self-destruction directly, and antibodies that carry toxins to cancer cells. These are different jobs, so a shared label of targeted does not make the mechanisms interchangeable, and a target that is only an address for delivery need not drive the cancer's growth.

An altered gene or an elevated protein can suggest a target hypothesis; it does not show that inhibiting the target will harm cancer cells selectively, which controlled perturbations of the target test, and safe exposure and appropriate clinical studies answer later questions. Naming a target answers only the first of several questions. Binding is an interaction between molecules and can be shown with a purified protein, which does not show that the compound reaches the protein inside a cell. Target engagement asks whether the interaction occurs in the relevant cells or tissue, and exposure, target location and the cell membrane all bear on it; a blood concentration and a concentration at an intracellular target are different observations. The cellular thermal shift assay of Martinez Molina and colleagues was developed to evaluate drug binding to target proteins in cells and tissue samples, and its authors used it to monitor drug transport and activation, off-target effects and resistance in cancer cell lines. Binding is also different from changing function: a compound can inhibit an enzyme, activate a receptor or deliver a payload, and a binder can leave the target's activity unchanged. Binding assays test an interaction under specified conditions and engagement assays examine the relevant cells or tissue, while a downstream signal measures a biological consequence and is not automatically a direct measure of how much of the target is occupied; growth, death and regrowth assays add further layers. A measured change in signalling, division or survival needs controls that test the proposed explanation, and one positive experiment should not carry the whole claim.

The last step is clinical. Mechanistic plausibility does not show benefit, because the target may also be present in healthy tissue and the useful margin depends on achieved benefit and harm in a stated disease, treatment setting, product and outcome. The National Cancer Institute adds that cancer cells can become resistant to targeted therapy when the target itself changes so the drug can no longer interact with it, or when cells find new ways to grow that do not depend on the target.

Worked example, fictional. An antibody binds protein A on cancer cells, and a growth assay shows no change. Binding is supported under the assay conditions. It has not been shown that protein A drives growth, that the antibody inhibits protein A's function, that a finished payload-bearing product delivers anything, or that the product is safe and beneficial; each of those needs its own evidence. Before saying a drug worked, name the layer that was measured.

records.name: Half-life
records.tldr: A half-life describes how long a specified drug concentration takes to fall by half under stated conditions; it does not by itself determine a treatment interval or when an effect ends.
records.summary:
A drug's half-life describes a halving of the concentration of a named substance in a specified phase or model. Early distribution, terminal elimination and the effective half-life relevant to accumulation can differ. With nonlinear elimination, a reported value can also depend on the dose. The December 2016 FDA clinical-pharmacology labelling guidance distinguishes effective from terminal half-life and asks for the conditions needed to interpret each.

Concentration and effect need separate measurements. Active metabolites, persistent biological changes and tissue injury can matter after the measured parent drug has declined. Living cell products can expand rather than simply disappear, and a radiopharmaceutical combines physical decay with biological removal. A half-life alone supplies no universal treatment schedule or recovery clock.

notes: Which half-life? A half-life describes a halving of concentration of a named substance in a named phase or model, and early distribution and terminal decline can differ. FDA labelling guidance says the half-life reported should usually be the effective half-life, based on the time to reach steady state, with a long terminal half-life noted where it matters for safety or effectiveness; for radiopharmaceuticals the effective half-life takes both the physical and the biological half-life into account (FDA, 'Oncology Therapeutic Radiopharmaceuticals: Nonclinical Studies and Labeling Recommendations'). It is not a clock for how long benefit or harm lasts, since downstream effects can persist after exposure falls, and a freely circulating drug's half-life does not describe cell products.

records.name: HER2
records.tldr: A growth-signal receptor. Some cancers make far too much of it, and drugs that block it or use it as a docking site have transformed those cancers.
records.summary: Human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 is a receptor tyrosine kinase amplified in ~15-20% of breast cancers and a subset of gastric, colorectal, lung (mutations), and biliary cancers. Trastuzumab (1998) was the first targeted antibody in solid tumours. Trastuzumab deruxtecan redefined the target by working in 'HER2-low' tumours that older drugs ignored, and in 2026 gained approval in early-stage disease.

notes: HER2 need not be drawn with a growth factor binding directly to it. Diwanji and colleagues' 2021 structural study examined a HER2-HER3 complex with neuregulin-1 beta bound to HER3. It describes HER2 as an orphan, ligand-less receptor and shows how the two receptors form their interface. Binding of a therapeutic antibody to HER2 is a different interaction from growth-factor binding to HER3. This structural experiment does not by itself identify a tumour's dependence or predict a clinical response.

Triple-negative breast cancer, HER2-low and ultralow: HER2-low (IHC 1+ or 2+/ISH-negative) in 36.6% of TNBC among 3,689 HER2-negative patients (Schettini 2021) and 34.0% of 1,162 hormone receptor-negative trial patients (Denkert 2021); HER2-null 38.4%, ultralow 37.6% and low 24.0% of 367 untreated TNBCs (Boissiere-Michot 2026). DESTINY-Breast04 enrolled 63 hormone receptor-negative patients (Modi 2022) and the HER2-low label covers them; DESTINY-Breast06 and the ultralow label are hormone receptor-positive only. In TNBC no gene separates HER2-low from HER2-0 and pathologist agreement is poor (Schettini 2021).

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma: ERBB2 amplification in 1 to 5% by platform and mutation in under 1% (cBioPortal); amplification in 2.2% of KRAS wild-type tumours (Philip 2022). It was among the druggable focal amplifications found at low individual prevalence in 100 whole genomes (Waddell 2015); zenocutuzumab reaches HER2 as the docking arm of its NRG1-blocking mechanism rather than as an amplified driver.

Colorectal cancer: ERBB2 amplification in 2 to 3% of all tumours but 5.3% of RAS and BRAF wild-type ones, which is the population that matters because it overlaps exactly with the patients an EGFR antibody would otherwise be given to (cBioPortal; Richman 2016; 48 of 914 screened for HERACLES). The threshold is the HERACLES criterion, intense membranous staining in more than 50% of cells corresponding to homogeneous amplification, not the 10% used in gastric cancer (Valtorta 2015). HER2 amplification was first proposed as a cause of cetuximab resistance in patient-derived xenografts (Bertotti 2011), and the regimens that followed are trastuzumab plus lapatinib (HERACLES, 30% response), tucatinib plus trastuzumab (MOUNTAINEER) and trastuzumab deruxtecan (DESTINY-CRC02). Plasma HER2 copy number selects patients as well as tissue does (Nakamura 2021). ERBB2 point mutations, 4 to 6%, are mostly passengers in hypermutated tumours and do not qualify.

Gallbladder cancer, amplification versus mutation: ERBB2 alterations were present in 14% of 260 patients, as 8% amplification alone, 4% mutation alone, 1.5% both and 0.4% fusion (Mondaca 2024, MSK-IMPACT), and in 15% of 376 Indian patients with about 8% amplification and an S310F/Y hotspot (Suryavanshi 2025). Only the amplified tumours are seen by IHC and ISH, which is what the zanidatamab label tests for (IHC 3+); the extracellular S310 and kinase-domain mutations need sequencing and are not covered by that label. Protein positivity depends on the scoring rule: 31.3% of 80 resected Japanese gallbladder carcinomas by the gastric guideline (Hiraoka 2020), 12.8% of 187 Chilean cases by breast criteria (Roa 2014), 9.4% of 53 by HERIZON-BTC-01 criteria (Angerilli 2026). ERBB2-driven biliary tumours can lose ERBB2 at progression (Cowzer 2026).

Lung cancer: a mutation target rather than an amplification target, the opposite of breast and stomach cancer. Exon 20 insertions are 1.9 to 2.2% of adenocarcinomas and 3.4% of never-smoker cases, with Y772_A775dup the dominant allele; any ERBB2 mutation reaches about 4%, and amplification, 1 to 3%, is a separate event that the licensed oral inhibitors do not select on (cBioPortal; Kris 2014). Amplification also appears as acquired resistance to EGFR blockade, in 3 of 24 rebiopsied patients (Yu 2013). Immunohistochemistry has no selective role here.

records.name: HER2-low and HER2-ultralow
records.tldr: HER2-low and HER2-ultralow describe particular staining categories used in breast-cancer studies and specified treatment labels. They do not mean that everyone in a category has the same biology or qualifies for the same treatment.
records.summary:
HER2-low generally denotes IHC 1+ or IHC 2+ with a negative ISH result in the relevant breast-cancer context. HER2-ultralow denotes the IHC 0 pattern with membrane staining used in DESTINY-Breast06 and the corresponding U.S. ENHERTU label. These are measured categories with assay and reporting context. The September 2026 CAP template records the membrane-staining pattern as negative score 0+, separately from negative score 0 with no detected membrane staining.

DESTINY-Breast04 studied previously chemotherapy-treated HER2-low metastatic disease, including hormone receptor-positive and hormone receptor-negative participants. DESTINY-Breast06 studied hormone receptor-positive disease after endocrine therapy without prior chemotherapy for metastatic disease; its primary comparison concerned HER2-low disease and its ultralow analysis was exploratory. Neither trial establishes that every low-expression category is one biological disease or validates a cutoff for every ADC. The U.S. ENHERTU HER2-low and HER2-ultralow breast indications require an FDA-authorized HER2 test and unresectable or metastatic disease. One use is HR-positive HER2-low or HER2-ultralow disease that has progressed on one or more endocrine therapies in the metastatic setting. A separate HER2-low use requires prior chemotherapy in the metastatic setting, or recurrence during or within six months after adjuvant chemotherapy. The latter low-expression use does not require HR-positive disease; the ultralow indication does. The score alone does not establish eligibility or individual benefit.

That is a result of that study, not the probability that an individual report is wrong. Tissue, sampling time, reader and assay matter; a second review or a different specimen needs clinical and laboratory context and does not guarantee a changed result or access to a medicine.

HER2-low generally means IHC 1+ or 2+/ISH-negative in the specified breast-cancer context. The faint incomplete pattern historically within IHC 0 and described as ultralow is separately recorded as negative 0+ in the September 2026 CAP template. Low expression is not the same as HER2 overexpression/amplification and is not necessarily one biological disease. Keep the actual test, integrated result, sample date and treatment setting; one score does not promise response to every antibody-drug conjugate.

Denkert's 2021 pooled analysis included 2,310 patients with HER2-non-amplified primary breast cancer treated in four prospective neoadjuvant chemotherapy trials. HER2-low meant IHC 1+ or 2+/ISH-negative. Among the 1,162 hormone receptor-negative tumours, 395 were HER2-low, about 34.0%. That is a tested category in this selected population, not a different HER2 protein, a universal TNBC prevalence or an independent treatment-eligibility rule.

Expression and clinical eligibility are different from organ-risk assessment. The U.S. ENHERTU label calls for assessment of left-ventricular ejection fraction before treatment and at regular intervals during treatment as clinically indicated. It does not turn a HER2 score into a personal monitoring schedule or establish that a tumour-expression category predicts cardiac injury.

The 2026 WHO review describes changes in HER2 reporting after DESTINY-Breast04 and DESTINY-Breast06. The September 2026 CAP template distinguishes score 0 with no detected membrane staining from score 0+ with faint incomplete membrane staining in 10 percent or fewer tumour cells. The template itself is not required for accreditation. The reporting category, the drug label and an individual’s clinical eligibility are separate; not every trace-staining result in every breast-cancer setting has the same treatment implication.

records.name: Linker (ADC)
records.tldr: The linker connects antibody and payload. Its chemistry affects where the drug separates and which active chemical species becomes available.
records.summary: Cleavable linkers can respond to enzymes, reduction or hydrolysis under specified conditions. Release is construct-specific and need not occur exclusively inside a cancer cell. A noncleavable linker can remain on the payload while the antibody is broken down, leaving an active amino-acid-linker-payload catabolite. For T-DM1, Lys-SMCC-DM1 must leave the lysosome to reach its intracellular site of action; SLC46A3 directly transports this catabolite in experimental systems. The released species can differ from the unconjugated parent drug in transport and permeability.

notes: The T-DM1 catabolite has low membrane permeability in the cited comparison; that is not a chemical rule that every noncleavable catabolite is impermeable. Bystander activity depends on release, diffusion, local concentration and neighboring-cell susceptibility. Linker hydrophilicity can mitigate hydrophobicity in particular designs without guaranteeing freedom from aggregation or toxicity.

In a fictional controlled comparison, Models A and B have similar measured binding and uptake, but B has less active material at the payload action site and more surviving cells later. The measured difference is after uptake; it does not uniquely identify the linker, because processing, transport and other model differences remain possible. Testing free active material with verified exposure at its action site can help: a response supports investigating delivery or processing, while persistent insensitivity motivates tests of payload action and cellular response. Neither result selects a treatment for a person.

Goldenberg and colleagues, working at Immunomedics, studied SG release of SN-38 in serum at 37 degrees Celsius. Their 2020 correction changed the human-serum release half-life from 23.98 to 18.82 hours after a data-entry error. They proposed contributions from intracellular delivery and local extracellular release. That preclinical chemistry and delivery rationale is not a direct map of release in a human tumour or the same parameter as the conjugate's human elimination half-life. Active drug still needs adequate local exposure and susceptible cells; it does not necessarily kill wherever it travels.

records.name: On-target, off-tumour toxicity and off-target cross-reactivity
records.tldr: On-target, off-tumour toxicity is harm to healthy tissue that carries the same target a treatment was built to recognise, so accurate recognition injures the tissue as well as the cancer.
records.summary:
On-target, off-tumour toxicity is injury from recognition of the intended target on healthy tissue. It differs from recognition of an unintended molecular target. The predictable, lymphoma-specific consequences of aiming at lineage antigens (B-cell aplasia, low immunoglobulin, and the effects of CD52, CCR4 and CD47 targeting) are described in the record on the cost of aiming at a lineage antigen, which this record does not repeat.

Many candidate cancer targets are normal proteins found at different levels or places in the body, so tumour-associated does not mean tumour-exclusive. A treatment that recognises its intended target wherever it is accessible, such as a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell, can harm any healthy tissue that displays it, and tissue location, target density, receptor properties and exposure all shape the outcome. This differs from off-target cross-reactivity, in which the receptor recognises an unintended molecule, and from cytokine release syndrome, which is systemic inflammatory activation; the three can occur together. It also differs from payload toxicity in an antibody-drug conjugate: a pooled analysis of ADC trials found the key grade 3 to 4 toxicities grouped by payload and concluded they were likely off-target and related to the payload (Masters et al., 2018). Binding specificity is not tissue selectivity, and experience with an antibody against a target does not automatically carry over to a living cell with a different recognition and signalling system.

Two primary reports show the contrast. A patient with colon cancer metastatic to the lungs and liver received 10 billion autologous T cells expressing a trastuzumab-based CAR against ERBB2 (HER2), the largest number permitted in the first dose-escalation cohort, the day after a lymphodepleting regimen of cyclophosphamide (60 mg/kg daily for 2 days) and fludarabine (25 mg/m2 for 5 days). Within 15 minutes the patient had respiratory distress, chest imaging showed pulmonary oedema, and the patient died 5 days after treatment, with marked rises in interferon-gamma, GM-CSF, tumour necrosis factor-alpha, interleukin-6 and interleukin-10. At autopsy multiple organs showed systemic ischaemia and haemorrhagic microangiopathic injury and the lungs diffuse alveolar damage; histological examination of autopsy tissue found ERBB2 at 3+ in liver metastases and 2+ in lung metastases and much lower levels in normal lung parenchyma, normal liver and normal breast. The authors hypothesised that highly active ERBB2-directed T cells recognised ERBB2 on normal lung cells on first pass through the lung and released inflammatory cytokines that began a cascade ending in multiorgan failure; the autopsy findings were read as initial lung injury followed by days of hypotension and ischaemia, and the authors call the significance of the cells' reactivity against cultured primary cells unclear. This is a single case, with a stated dose and conditioning, whose mechanism is the authors' hypothesis and which gives no incidence for any CAR product (Morgan et al., 2010). In a trial of an affinity-enhanced T-cell receptor against HLA-A*01-restricted MAGE-A3 in myeloma and melanoma, the first two patients developed cardiogenic shock and died within days; no MAGE-A3 expression was detected in heart tissue at autopsy, and beating cardiomyocytes made from induced pluripotent stem cells triggered T-cell killing through recognition of an unrelated peptide from titin. That is off-target recognition of an unintended molecule, not the intended target in the wrong tissue (Linette et al., 2013).

How the question is asked before and during trials. FDA's CAR T-cell development guidance says to assess both undesired targeting of healthy tissue that expresses the intended antigen (on-target/off-tumour) and unintended targeting of other antigens, using examples such as tissue cross-reactivity studies with an antibody carrying the same recognition domain, protein arrays, cytotoxicity and cytokine-release testing on panels of primary cells, cell lines or stem-cell-derived organ systems, and relevant animal models, and encourages a combination of methods; antigen recognition domains can differ in affinity or avidity or recognise a different site, which should be evaluated, and CAR T cells can carry added components such as suicide genes. In practice a readout is a staining intensity or positive fraction, a binding profile, killing or cytokine release by healthy cells at a named time, and finally organ injury in the treated population; stained fixed tissue does not show a living organ's accessibility, an animal model may lack the human target, and a negative result in one panel is not a safety certificate. No universal expression cut-off is given here because no source read gives one. Whether affinity tuning, recognition logic or control switches improve safety for a particular design needs that design's own evidence. The 2026 ASTCT consensus abstract lists on-target, off-tumour toxicity among the toxicities for which it considered definitions and grading; its criteria were not readable.

If it also recognises Y on an X-negative healthy cell, that is off-target cross-reactivity. Binding or surface contact does not itself measure injury. Record tissue, assay sensitivity, staining intensity, positive fraction or calibrated molecules per cell, binding specificity, and healthy-cell killing or cytokine release at a named time; viable-cell tests consume the sample. Clinical organ injury is a further outcome in the actual population and regimen. A staining ratio, one negative panel or a control switch does not establish safety everywhere or guarantee reversal of an injury already present.

records.name: Payload (ADC)
records.tldr: A payload is the active cargo carried by a delivery product. Its identity and action are different from the molecule used to reach a target.
records.summary: Cytotoxic antibody-drug conjugates carry an active small-molecule drug attached to an antibody. Examples include the topoisomerase I inhibitors SN-38 and DXd and the microtubule-directed drugs MMAE and DM1. The complete product, its attachment chemistry and the chemical species released after processing matter alongside the nominal payload class. Membrane permeability can contribute to local bystander activity, but permeability alone does not establish neighbouring-cell exposure, killing, tumour coverage or clinical benefit.

notes: Class effects versus product figures. US labels report brentuximab vedotin peripheral neuropathy of any grade in 62 per cent of patients in monotherapy studies; mirvetuximab soravtansine ocular adverse reactions in 59 per cent of patients with ovarian cancer, grade 3 in 11 per cent; belantamab mafodotin dosage modification for ocular toxicity in 83 per cent of patients in its clinical study, with a boxed warning and a restricted programme; and tisotumab vedotin a boxed warning for severe ocular toxicity, including severe vision loss and corneal ulceration, with an ophthalmic examination before every cycle for the first nine. Datopotamab deruxtecan: stomatitis in 63 per cent and ocular adverse reactions in 38 per cent of 1,365 patients treated as a single agent at 6 mg/kg in the pooled label population. Trastuzumab emtansine carries a boxed warning for hepatotoxicity, cardiac toxicity and embryo-fetal toxicity. The sacituzumab govitecan, trastuzumab deruxtecan and trastuzumab emtansine rates, and the datopotamab deruxtecan lung-disease rates, are in the record on ADC side effects in breast cancer. The figures come from different trials and populations and cannot be compared head to head, and sharing a payload class does not make products equivalent.

A new strategy is a hypothesis about a specified failure. A different microtubule-directed payload tests another action; a redesigned TOP1 payload can change transport or potency while retaining vulnerabilities. A repair or checkpoint inhibitor proposes changing the response to damage and remains a chemical intervention. A transcription inhibitor needs drug- and model-specific evidence, including any claim about noncycling cells. An immune-stimulating conjugate needs evidence for useful immune activation, its harms and any durable effect after exposure ends. Alpha-emitter proposals still need carrier distribution, retention, radiation dose and response evidence. Two-address or biparatopic binding can change delivery, but neither uniquely exhausts delivery strategies nor guarantees productive uptake. These categories overlap; a diagram does not establish exclusive failure classes or rank how predictable their safety will be.

For any proposed cargo, state its biological bet, why antibody delivery might improve on the active material alone, and what would falsify the explanation. Then separate adequate loading and exposure, appropriate resistant models, functional target or response measurements, heterogeneous tumour coverage, normal-tissue effects and a clinical comparison matching the claim. One study does not settle mechanism, safety and benefit at once. Immune memory, rescue of resistance and clinical superiority need their own results rather than being consequences of a platform name.

In a fictional Company B report, a repair- or checkpoint-directed conjugate has model activity and six dose-escalation patients, without a comparative benefit result. Ask whether the intended response pathway was changed at adequate exposure, with what harm, and whether the proposed biomarker modifies treatment effect in an appropriate comparison. Responses concentrated in one marker group do not alone prove predictive validity or mechanism; responses scattered across groups do not alone disprove a mechanism.

In a separate fictional checkpoint-payload report, four shrinkages among 18 patients describe uncontrolled activity. They do not establish improved survival, a validated biomarker or the cause of each response. A post-TOP1 claim needs the earlier agents and actual progression history; interpret dose-limiting harm, active exposure and target or response measurements separately. A meaningful active-material comparison and full-conjugate comparison can test the delivery rationale. Neither the small response count nor one experiment settles all these questions.

records.name: Pharmacokinetics (PK), half-life and exposure
records.tldr: Pharmacokinetics follows a named medicine or its components through the body by measuring concentration over time, which differs from both the amount administered and the biological effect.
records.summary:
Pharmacokinetics describes absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion. A dose is an administered amount; exposure describes a named substance's concentration over time in a specified compartment. Route, organ function, metabolism, binding and interactions can make equal doses produce different exposure.

The December 2016 FDA labelling guidance asks for measures such as maximum plasma concentration, concentration-time area under the curve, clearance, accumulation and half-life in their relevant conditions. These measurements inform dosage selection alongside activity, safety and tolerability; they do not establish benefit on their own. For conjugated drugs, active metabolites and radiopharmaceuticals, specify which component was measured. Blood concentration is not automatically the concentration of active material at a cancer-cell target.

notes: Dose, exposure and effect are three different things. Dose is the administered amount; exposure is a named substance's concentration over time in a named place, which route, organ function, interactions and product properties can change for the same dose; and effect is a separate measurement, because effects or injury can persist after exposure falls and detectable drug does not guarantee productive engagement. Pharmacokinetics follows absorption (including how much of an oral dose reaches the circulation), distribution (plasma is not the unbound concentration inside a cell), metabolism (active metabolites may add their own exposure) and excretion, summarised by clearance, the removal relative to concentration, in volume per time. FDA labelling guidance lists the maximum plasma concentration (Cmax) and area under the concentration-time curve (AUC) at the approved dosage, time to steady state, accumulation ratio, clearance, volume of distribution and half-life; this AUC is an exposure area and is unrelated to the area under a prediction curve that judges tests.

For an antibody-drug conjugate, specify whether an assay follows conjugated antibody, total antibody, unconjugated payload or an active breakdown product. The 2024 FDA guidance defines total antibody as antibody with or without attached payload and discusses relevant constituent parts, metabolites and catabolites. Their concentration histories can differ: persistent antibody signal does not establish active payload in every cancer cell. Living cell products can expand or persist, and a radioligand combines radioactive decay with biological removal, so a freely circulating drug's half-life gives no universal clock for them.

Read the measurement card as well as the curve. Record the dose, route, analyte, sampled compartment, assay, population and sampling interval. Concentration can be in ng/mL, maximum concentration in the same units, concentration-time area in ng·hour/mL, half-life in hours and clearance in litres per hour. Sampling should capture the phase of interest: a sparse late sample cannot reliably recover an unobserved early peak. Pharmacodynamics measures biological effects separately. First-pass metabolism can reduce oral bioavailability; protein binding and active metabolites also matter.

The fictional halving example assumes one compartment, stopped input and a constant four-hour half-life. Its four markers are model values, not observed samples: 100, 50, 25 and 12.5 ng/mL at 0, 4, 8 and 12 hours. Integrating that exponential only from 0 to 12 hours gives about 505 ng·hour/mL, not the lifetime area, administered dose or biological effect. The example supplies no safe next-treatment time.

A fictional six-month research plan measures neither a batch's manufacturing lead time nor the duration of drug action. Designing and testing a candidate, making and quality-releasing a specified batch, and observing exposure and effects after dosing are three different clocks. A laboratory binder may never become a clinically usable product. Ask separately whether material is ready, a clinical use is authorised, eligibility is met and an appropriate site can provide it; a calendar estimate does not answer those questions. Repeated protein doses and preparation of a person's cell product are different tasks. Research dependencies can overlap without establishing that concurrent treatments are effective, safe or authorised. For the dosing clock, ask which schedule and monitoring are supported for the actual product and setting.

records.name: Radioligand therapy (beta emitters)
records.tldr: A target-binding molecule carries a radionuclide whose emissions deposit radiation in tissue. Distribution and retention help determine tumor and normal-organ exposure.
records.summary: Lutetium-177 therapies deliver beta-particle radiation through target-binding molecules. VISION tested PSMA-targeted treatment added to protocol-permitted standard care in selected, previously treated metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer. NETTER-1 tested lutetium-177-dotatate in progressive, somatostatin-receptor-positive midgut neuroendocrine tumors. Their clinical results belong to those populations and products, rather than every tumor expressing the target. Small molecules, peptides and antibodies have different distribution and clearance even when directed at a shared target.

Dosimetry combines suitable activity measurements or models over time with tissue geometry and emission properties. Neither the targeting-molecule mass nor the administered activity alone specifies tumor dose.

Radioimmunotherapy uses an antibody carrier. The broader radiopharmaceutical category also includes organ-seeking products without a separate targeting ligand. Not every attachment uses a metal chelator. Alpha and beta emissions have different path and energy-deposition properties; neither label alone ranks safety or effectiveness. Daughter redistribution and microscopic geometry can matter.

Radiation can deposit energy beyond the cell carrying the radioactive product, so chemical-payload uptake into each neighbouring cell is not the same requirement. Binding and internalisation can affect retention, but the complete carrier's distribution, biological removal, radionuclide decay and tissue geometry still determine delivery. A diagnostic tracer image is not a measured therapeutic absorbed dose, and resistance to a chemotherapy payload does not itself establish radiation sensitivity or safe organ exposure.

The isotope and range convention matter; one beta or alpha number is not a value for every radionuclide. FDA's 2019 radiopharmaceutical guidance separately defines physical, biological and effective half-life and time-integrated activity.

records.name: T-cell engagers (bispecific)
records.tldr: T-cell engagers are proteins that bind a specified target and recruit T cells, often through CD3. A binding bridge does not by itself establish completed killing.
records.summary:
A dosed T-cell engager supplies a protein connecting target recognition to an available T cell. It does not itself install receptor instructions or supply engineered living responders. Product design can use antibody-derived binding fragments or a soluble TCR recognition domain; some target arms require a particular peptide-HLA complex. Compact BiTE designs, Fc-containing architectures and half-life extension describe features that can overlap rather than mutually exclusive treatment categories.

Clinical examples include blinatumomab in B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia, teclistamab in multiple myeloma and tarlatamab in extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer. Their actual labels define different settings, combinations, prior treatments and harms. Tebentafusp is a peptide-HLA-directed soluble TCR/CD3 protein with its own allele- and disease-specific use. Neither a common platform name nor binding in a laboratory establishes eligibility or comparative benefit.

notes: An antibody-derived TCR mimic recognizes a peptide-HLA complex using an antibody scaffold. A soluble TCR/CD3 engager instead uses a TCR-derived recognition scaffold attached to a recruiting arm. TCR-T administers cells carrying receptor chains. Target recognition, molecular scaffold and administered object are separate axes; a mimic can be part of an engager without becoming a TCR protein.

Liddy studied soluble TCR/CD3 ImmTAC proteins in experimental systems. Dao studied an antibody-derived WT1/HLA-A*02:01/CD3 engager in cells and mice. Their results do not establish clinical benefit for every scaffold, HLA allele or cancer. Recruiting another T cell does not require that cell’s native receptor to recognize the target, but does not remove the target arm’s HLA restriction.

The KIMMTRAK label identifies tebentafusp as a soluble gp100 peptide-HLA/CD3 protein for HLA-A*02:01-positive adults with unresectable or metastatic uveal melanoma. This is a named clinical protein example, not an engineered-cell product or evidence that other peptide-HLA binders share its indication or outcomes.

Binding to supplied peptide-HLA reagent can bypass natural processing and display. Source-protein expression or a compatible genotype alone is not a functional target assay. For a research claim, compare naturally presenting targets, irrelevant peptides, the wrong HLA allele, antigen-negative targets, suitable effector cells, no-effector conditions and healthy tissues. Labeled clinical selection tests remain a separate clinical-use rule. Record the peptide sequence, HLA allele, display method and its detection or recovery limits; no universal target-density cutoff follows from the format name.

The Mack construct joined two single-chain Fv fragments with a peptide linker in one compact protein; this is different from an IgG architecture with an Fc region. The FDA tarlatamab application describes DLL3/CD3 binding domains combined with an IgG Fc region in a half-life-extended BiTE. Thus BiTE, Fc-containing and half-life-extended are not three exclusive buckets. Fc design, binding geometry, affinity, target density, distribution and measured exposure still belong to the specific molecule. The Giffin cell, mouse and nonhuman-primate study does not define a universal human schedule.

Compare recognition, T-cell activation, proliferation, target death, cytokine release and protein exposure at named times. Record effector source/state, target density, effector-to-target ratio, dose or concentration and denominator; include target-negative and no-effector controls. A granule or cytokine signal does not substitute for completed target-cell death or clinical benefit. Cytokines in a culture are a measured laboratory endpoint, not a diagnosis of clinical cytokine-release syndrome.

Bluemel compared epitope positions and antigen sizes in engineered cell systems. Constructs with similar target-binding affinity differed in target-cell lysis, supporting functional testing of the actual geometry rather than ranking every molecule by affinity alone. In the solitomab phase 1 solid-tumor study, dose-limiting diarrhea and liver abnormalities constrained dose escalation; an accessible target and a binding bridge did not by themselves establish a useful therapeutic window.

Compared with administered CAR-T or TCR-T cells, a protein engager recruits effectors rather than supplying engineered responders. Protein mass/concentration and viable-cell dose have different units; clearance differs from cell survival, expansion and trafficking. A shared target name does not establish matched epitope, affinity, contact geometry, exposure, controllability or safety.

The 2025 FDA tarlatamab decision followed the randomized DeLLphi-304 comparison after platinum-based treatment in SCLC. Its survival finding belongs to that drug and setting. The cited blinatumomab consolidation and teclistamab combination/monotherapy decisions likewise retain their own settings; none is a class-wide treatment-sequencing rule.

Stopping a protein infusion and reversing an injury are different outcomes. In Kebenko's 2018 phase 1 solitomab study of 65 patients with refractory solid tumours, the reported half-life was 4.5 hours. Diarrhoea limited dosing; one grade 3 event progressed to grade 5 after solitomab discontinuation. That observation shows why short measured protein exposure does not guarantee immediate reversal of toxicity. It is one product and study, not a rate or a safety rule for all engagers. Living engineered cells have their own expansion, persistence and trafficking, rather than sharing this protein's clearance clock.

For a lymphoma engager, target presence, access to suitable T cells and useful effector function need separate evidence. Antigen expression alone does not establish these other steps. These biological questions do not by themselves select an earlier treatment line; treatment timing needs evidence for the actual drug and setting.

Protein exposure can be adjusted through a specified dosing regimen
limitations: Productive encounters need accessible targets and functional effectors
Healthy-tissue recognition, cytokine release and neurologic harms need product-specific evidence
Stopping administration does not instantly clear protein or reverse an effect already triggered

records.name: T-cell receptor
records.tldr: A conventional T-cell receptor recognises a peptide together with its HLA display. Recognition alone does not show killing.
records.summary:
A conventional alpha-beta T-cell receptor uses paired chains to recognise a peptide-HLA surface. Its recognition chains assemble with CD3 signalling partners, as demonstrated in the human TCR-CD3 structural study. CDR3 is an informative variable region, but neither a beta-chain sequence nor CDR3 alone specifies the complete paired receptor or its function.

Particular receptors can cross-react across peptide and HLA contexts; that does not establish a universal cross-reactivity rate. Paired receptor identity, binding, activation, target-cell death and clinical benefit require different evidence. A response by one reconstructed pair to peptide-loaded cells does not establish that another alpha-chain pairing recognises the same target, or that either kills naturally presenting tumour cells. Use irrelevant-target, HLA and target-only viability controls. Peptide loading can bypass natural processing, and contact diagrams are not healthy-tissue safety tests.

CD3 signalling partners are distinct from recognition chains. Contact loops including junction-spanning CDR3 contribute, but other loops, the partner chain and HLA matter; beta-only or CDR3-only sequence is incomplete.

Cross-reactivity is recognition of multiple targets by a receptor. Defined receptor experiments demonstrated peptide/HLA cross-reactivity, not recognition of every allele by an arbitrary receptor or a universal rate. Greater affinity or a contact drawing does not establish healthy-tissue safety.

Sequencing reports sampled receptor identities and abundances under an operational clonotype definition. Paired alpha-beta identities are more complete than beta alone. Peptide-HLA multimer binding, stimulus-induced cellular response, target-cell death and clinical benefit are different endpoints. Include irrelevant-target, HLA and target-only viability controls; peptide-loaded cells can bypass natural processing.

Vaccination generally recruits or expands existing mature receptor specificities rather than rewriting each mature receptor. Engineered TCR therapy introduces selected receptor sequences. In either case, tested recognition must still connect to naturally presenting tumour targets, useful function and healthy-tissue safety. If one beta sequence pairs with different alpha chains, a positive reconstruction of one pair does not establish the other pair's function or tumour killing.

records.name: Targeted therapy
records.tldr: A targeted treatment acts on a specified molecule or process. Some block a cancer dependence; others use a molecule as an address for delivery or immune recruitment. The target name alone does not establish benefit or normal-tissue safety.
records.summary:
Targeted treatments include small molecules and therapeutic antibodies with different actions. A molecule whose function supports cancer growth and a surface molecule used to deliver an active drug or recruit an immune cell have different roles. Detecting either does not by itself establish that the finished treatment reaches its target, changes a relevant function or helps in a particular clinical setting.

Some treatments require a specified biomarker test; others have no target-expression selection test in the relevant label. Keep the actual drug, disease, treatment setting and testing rule together. NCI describes resistance and potentially serious adverse effects of targeted therapy. Neither relative normal-tissue sparing, mild toxicity nor a permanent response follows from the word targeted.

A molecule used as an address for delivery and a molecule whose function the cell depends on are different roles.

Targeted therapy was once expected to be less toxic than chemotherapy but can cause serious side effects, cancer cells can become resistant to it, and it may work best combined with other targeted therapy or with treatments such as chemotherapy and radiation (NCI page, HTML read).

records.name: Tebentafusp
records.tldr: The first drug to improve survival in metastatic uveal melanoma, and the first TCR-based bispecific.
records.summary: Tebentafusp is an ImmTAC: a soluble, affinity-enhanced T-cell receptor that recognises a gp100 peptide presented on HLA-A*02:01, fused to an anti-CD3 single-chain antibody that recruits available functional T cells to cells displaying the specified complex. Because gp100 is a melanocyte-lineage protein, the drug also hits skin melanocytes, so rash and pruritus are expected. It is given weekly after step-up doses of 20, 30 and 68 micrograms, with inpatient monitoring for the first three doses because of cytokine release syndrome and hypotension. Approved in 2022 in the US and EU for HLA-A*02:01-positive metastatic uveal melanoma, it was the first drug to improve survival in that disease (overall survival 21.7 versus 16.0 months) and the first TCR-based bispecific approved anywhere. It is being tested in cutaneous melanoma after PD-1 therapy (TEBE-AM), and Immunocore's PRAME-directed brenetafusp follows the same design.

records.name: Therapeutic index (therapeutic window)
records.tldr: Therapeutic index is a ratio comparing doses that produce defined toxic and useful effects; a therapeutic window is a range, and neither is a personal guarantee of safety.
records.summary:
A formal therapeutic index divides a dose producing a specified toxic effect by a dose producing a specified useful effect in stated experimental conditions. It is dimensionless when the dose units are compatible. A therapeutic window instead describes a range of doses or concentrations meeting stated activity and harm criteria. Always retain the effect definitions, population, time and uncertainty.

Low-concentration activity, target binding or a wider margin in a laboratory assay does not establish clinical safety. Distribution, formulation, schedule, other medicines and longer-term effects can change the relationship. The August 2024 FDA oncology dosage-optimisation guidance considers exposure, activity, safety and tolerability together, rather than assuming that the highest tolerated dose must be optimal. Its scope is stated for particular development settings and does not supply one rule for every treatment modality.

Hamblett et al., effects of drug loading on a monoclonal antibody-drug conjugate (2004)
FDA: optimizing the dosage of drugs for oncologic diseases (August 2024 guidance)
