notes: A laboratory margin depends on which useful and harmful effects were tested, in which populations and over what time. A measure built on one toxicity can miss another. Different conditions in tumour-cell and normal-cell assays also limit transfer to people. A more selective result in one pair of cultures supports that assay comparison, not a general clinical safety claim. FDA's narrow-therapeutic-index discussion concerns small changes in dose or concentration causing treatment failure or serious harm; it does not classify all chemotherapy as one regulatory group.

Payload and loading change the margin. In one mouse study of anti-CD30 MMAE conjugates with 2, 4 or 8 drugs per antibody, the 4-loaded conjugate's antitumour activity matched the 8-loaded at equal antibody dose, the maximum tolerated dose of the 2-loaded was at least double that of the 4-loaded, which was twice that of the 8-loaded, and the 8-loaded cleared 3-fold faster than the 4-loaded; lower loading raised the therapeutic index for that conjugate (Hamblett et al.), which does not generalise to every ADC. FDA's August 2024 oncology dosage-optimisation guidance integrates exposure, activity, safety and tolerability, and says it does not specifically address radiopharmaceuticals, cellular and gene therapy products, oncolytic viruses, microbiota or cancer vaccines, or paediatric development.

A complete fictional ratio example specifies the same model-organism population, one administration and day-14 readouts. Useful effect is an invented decrease of at least two points on a 0-to-10 symptom score; toxicity is an injury marker at least twice baseline. Constructed curves reach 50% at doses 2 and 6, giving an index of 6/2 = 3. Separate, arbitrarily chosen criteria of at least 80% meeting the useful readout and at most 10% meeting the toxic readout give a dose range of about 2.83 to 3.46 on those curves. The range keeps dose units and depends on its criteria. No sampling uncertainty or acceptable clinical harm threshold is supplied.

In a fictional Company A report, a 100-fold potency difference in a specified cell assay and mouse regression are the observations; no patients have been treated. That potency ratio supplies neither a human benefit estimate nor a 100-fold change in marrow injury. Compare delivered active exposure, the relevant resistant models and useful and harmful effects under stated conditions. More potency does not itself demonstrate transport evasion, rescue of a target mutation or an improved therapeutic window. Human tolerability is a separate question.

records.name: Trastuzumab
records.tldr: The first targeted antibody for a solid tumour (1998), which turned HER2-positive breast cancer from the worst subtype into one of the most treatable.
records.summary: Trastuzumab is a humanised IgG1 antibody that binds domain IV of HER2, blocking receptor signalling and recruiting immune cells through ADCC. It was the first targeted antibody for a solid tumour, approved for HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer in 1998, as adjuvant therapy in 2006 (HERA, NSABP B-31/N9831, about a 37% reduction in death) and for HER2-positive gastric cancer in 2010. Dual blockade with pertuzumab (CLEOPATRA, APHINITY) and the subcutaneous Phesgo built on it, and it is the antibody backbone of the conjugates T-DM1 and T-DXd. Adjuvant treatment lasts 1 year, and cardiomyopathy requires LVEF monitoring. Biosimilars since 2017 have cut cost worldwide, and whether shorter adjuvant courses are safe for lower-risk patients remains debated. For a newcomer: the drug that turned the worst breast cancer subtype into one of the most treatable.

records.name: TROP2 expression
records.tldr: TROP2 expression is a measured feature, not a universal ADC selection rule. The current U.S. breast-cancer uses of sacituzumab govitecan and datopotamab deruxtecan do not require a TROP2 test; other treatment requirements still apply.
records.summary:
In ASCENT, a prespecified exploratory analysis used an immunohistochemical H-score to examine TROP2 expression. Results were available for 290 of the 468 patients in the primary population without brain metastases. The authors supported benefit in the high and medium groups and said the low group was too small for a definitive benefit conclusion. This analysis does not establish equal effects at every expression level or a validated universal threshold. A marker association, a randomised treatment comparison and a treatment-by-marker interaction answer different questions.

The current U.S. breast indications for sacituzumab govitecan and datopotamab deruxtecan do not require a TROP2 selection assay. That regulatory rule does not prove that the target or its delivery is biologically irrelevant. Check the exact drug, subtype, setting and prior treatment. The first-line sacituzumab-pembrolizumab regimen has a separate PD-L1 CPS requirement of at least 10 using an FDA-authorized test. A research H-score or computational membrane score is not automatically an interchangeable clinical selection test.

Two retrospective TNBC series used different assays. Jacot's 2025 nonmetastatic series used the Enzo ENZ-ABS380 antibody and H-scores below 100, 100 to 200, and above 200: 225 of 228 tumours had membrane expression and 58.8% were in the strong group. Izci's 2022 series included 685 patients overall, with 589 scored for these groups using Abcam ab227689: 97 high (201 to 300), 149 medium (100 to 200) and 343 low (below 100), or 16.5%, 25.3% and 58.2%. These are assay- and cohort-specific distributions, not harmonised prevalence estimates or validated individual treatment thresholds.

Stepan's 2011 transcript and protein survey found substantial TROP2 expression in several essential normal tissues. Tumour enrichment and a current label's lack of a TROP2 selection test answer different questions from accessible normal-tissue expression and the finished product's therapeutic window. A fictional 85%-positive, minimally normal-staining proposal still needs the antibody, cutoff, cohort, positive-cell distribution within tumours, normal tissues and methods, and full-product distribution, processing and response evidence. A single stain or an antigen count does not supply those results.

records.name: Immune-related adverse events (irAEs)
records.tldr: Checkpoint inhibitors can cause immune-related adverse events such as colitis, rash, hepatitis, pneumonitis and thyroid problems. Management depends on the organ and severity and may involve steroids, other immunosuppression or hormone replacement.
records.summary:
Immune-related adverse events are injuries attributed to treatment-related immune activity, commonly discussed with checkpoint inhibitors. They can affect the bowel, lung, skin, liver, hormone-producing glands and other organs. A symptom or laboratory change during treatment does not by itself establish an immune cause.

Clinical assessment identifies the organ, severity, timing and competing explanations. Reactions can arise after treatment stops, and some endocrine injury leaves lasting loss of function. Organ-specific management can include different measures, such as treatment interruption, immunosuppression or hormone replacement. An adverse event, an attributed immune injury and a cancer-response result are separate findings.

notes: What the label does and does not say. An adverse event is any unfavourable and unintended sign, symptom or abnormal laboratory finding that occurs during treatment, whether or not the treatment caused it; grading records that it occurred and how severe it was, and the clinical team assigns attribution to the drug, the intervention or something else (NCI Cancer Therapy Evaluation Program). An irAE is the narrower attribution of harm to treatment-related immune activity, so a symptom during immunotherapy is not automatically an irAE, and the abbreviation names a suspected mechanism, not an organ, a severity or a treatment. The SITC 2021 guideline uses the same wording, grades events including irAEs on a scale such as CTCAE version 5, and says that some irAEs need organ-specific management while overarching principles apply to all checkpoint-inhibitor toxicity. Checkpoint regulation helps limit responses against healthy tissue, part of peripheral tolerance; disrupting that protection can contribute to immune injury, but no single mechanism explains every event. Colitis names bowel inflammation and pneumonitis lung inflammation. A symptom or the suffix "-itis" does not establish its cause.

Timing and neighbouring syndromes. Immune-mediated reactions to PD-1 or PD-L1 antibodies can occur in any organ system at any time after starting and can also appear after treatment stops (pembrolizumab prescribing information), so the infusion calendar does not define the observation window; onset differs by organ, with a SITC median of 5 to 10 weeks for diarrhoea or colitis and rash typically presenting 2 to 5 weeks after the first treatment. Cytokine release syndrome and ICANS after immune effector cell therapy are separate syndromes with their own ASTCT definitions and grading, not substitute labels for checkpoint-related organ injury, and stopping a treatment does not guarantee the immune effect has stopped.

Report symptoms using the care team's plan and tell evaluating clinicians about current and previous immunotherapy. New or worsening breathing difficulty, chest pain or confusion can need urgent assessment. A person with a new cough after checkpoint treatment should neither dismiss the possible relationship because dosing ended nor infer pneumonitis without evaluation. The organ-inflammation guidance from NCI advises reporting concerning changes rather than waiting for another infusion or starting immune-suppressing treatment independently. Suspected immune injury does not show that the cancer treatment is working.

Pembrolizumab before and after surgery for triple-negative breast cancer: Macmillan says the treatment can make the immune system too active, that side effects can start during treatment or after it ends, and that glands making hormones (such as the thyroid) can be permanently affected, sometimes needing daily tablets. Breast Cancer Now says you should be given an alert card listing the symptoms to report and an out-of-hours contact.

The symptoms both charities ask you to report straight away on the 24-hour number: more stools than usual, stools at night, watery stools or tummy cramps (bowel inflammation); breathlessness, a cough that does not go away, wheeze or fever (lung inflammation); yellow skin or eyes, sickness (liver inflammation); unusual tiredness, headaches that do not go away, dizziness, thirst or passing more urine (hormone glands).

Lung cancer: checkpoint treatment is used at every stage of lung cancer, so the same warning list applies whether it is given before surgery, after chemoradiotherapy or for cancer that has spread. Macmillan says to contact the hospital straight away on the 24-hour number for breathlessness, a cough that does not go away, wheezing or a fever over 37.5 C (lung inflammation); for passing more stools than is normal for you or passing stools at night (bowel inflammation); for a spreading rash, blistering or peeling skin with flu-like symptoms; and for a temperature above 37.5 C or below 36 C or feeling unwell with a normal temperature. It also says these can start during treatment or after treatment ends, which is why the patient alert card is worth carrying.
